work.author: Origen
work.title: Fragmenta In Lamentationes (In Catenis de Prophetis)

paragraphs.text: The Fragments from the Catena on the Prophets.

When the people had been taken captive and were in Babylon, Jeremiah laments the city, the land and the people for what had befallen them. He laments by composing certain sections and divisions that begin, in order, with the letters of the Hebrew alphabet. After completing the lament on each letter, and last of all the one beginning with Tau, which is the final letter of the Hebrews, he returns to Aleph and laments again; and he does this four times, going through the twenty-two letters.

If we see the soul becoming subject to the devil or to his angels, and in a word to the hostile powers (the soul that by nature is contemplative and able to perceive the things that are and attend to them), we shall understand in some measure what the captivity is and who the captor is. But if we take refuge in Christ, who, according to the prophet Isaiah, proclaimed "release to the captives," we shall be set free from the captivity, even if the captor has gone so far as to bind us. For Jesus came "to bring the bound out of their bonds, and those who sit in darkness out of the prison house."

For this reason the Hebrews say that the books of the Old Testament are equal in number to the letters, so that they form a complete introduction to the knowledge of God, just as the letters are an introduction to all wisdom for those who learn. And for this reason the series is repeated four times, perhaps because the elements of bodies are also four.
And a little later:
No edition of Aquila or Theodotion is extant for Lamentations, but only those of Symmachus and the Seventy.
And again:

One might ask why, when the title of the book is in the plural, "Lamentations," he speaks in the prologue in the singular of "this lament." The answer is that, taken in parts, there are several laments, divided according to the letters, but they are all brought together into one, since they all refer to a single subject, Israel.
It is the weeping that comes from love that is called blessed. For it belongs to the saint "to weep with those who weep."

As the Lord drew near to Jerusalem, "he wept and said, If you too had known the things that make for your peace." "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you! How often I wanted to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were not willing."

If, then, "blessed are those who weep, for they shall laugh," Jeremiah had to weep this mystical weeping and, in keeping with "blessed are those who mourn," to mourn for those who deserved to be mourned.

As far as the letter goes, "the multitude of the people" seems to mean the Israelites who lived there, and "the multitude of the nations," as we said before, the proselytes. In the anagogical sense, since contemplative things are more akin to the soul and less bound by circumstance than practical things, the multitude of the people means the wealth of contemplations, and the multitude of the nations the great number of good deeds.
And a little later:
She who was full of people sits alone. Because the bride has cast off the Word, her bridegroom, she becomes like a widow, she who once was full of the nations mentioned before.

As far as the letter goes, it is fitting to understand that Jerusalem is spoken of with astonishment because of her change for the worse: she who was once full of people sits in isolation, so that her isolation is her desolation. She had as her husband the living Word, her protector, while she followed him as he was present and helping her; but she has been widowed and abandoned by him [?] for her sins.
And after other things:

So much for the literal sense. As to the meaning, Jerusalem, prospering, full of people and nations, and ruling over lands, is the divine soul. It is no wonder that the perfect soul is called neither merely a house, nor a farmstead, nor even the village, which is larger than these, nor any ordinary city, but Jerusalem, the city that surpasses all cities and is honored by God. For a remarkable greatness of wisdom and of all virtue surrounds it like the greatest of cities, † abounding in manifold buildings [?].
And a little later:

Just as one can see Jerusalem prospering, full of people and nations and ruling among the lands, so too, since virtue can be lost, one can see her at times left alone, widowed and enslaved, so that she even pays tribute to the enemy who has conquered her. This happens in the soul of one who has fallen away from the truth.

What need is there to speak of how she who ruled over lands is so enslaved to her enemies that she continually pays tribute, obeying [?] her masters in whatever they command? And they command nothing good. Perhaps for each fault she commits here she pays some tribute to Nebuchadnezzar, whose name means "Sitting-in" and "knowledge of constraint"; and not only to Nebuchadnezzar, but also to his satraps.

In the first lament, the one beginning with Aleph, we were able to keep to the literal sense. But here, what could one say, when a city is said to have wept in the night, so that its tears are on its cheeks? Unless one were to say that those who are called the city, the very ones who pay tribute, wept when they remembered from what peace and freedom they had come into such slavery and humiliation. How then shall we explain "in the night"? Perhaps at the time when all people commonly rest, the city remembered, and as they rested they wept, and wept with their tears streaming down their cheeks. Their weeping grew especially intense and their tears flowed because there was not even one of all those who loved her to comfort them, and every friend had broken off his friendship with her and turned to enmity. Who, then, in the literal sense, were those who formerly loved her, of whom none was there to comfort her? Perhaps the other cities of Judea, which perhaps loved the mother city for that reason, did not comfort her in her time of distress.
And a little later:

So much for the literal sense. If [?] the soul is said to weep, as in what came before, having fallen from its own land and come into Confusion, and to be in a state opposite to laughing the laughter of joy and cheerfulness, which our Lord promises will belong to those who have wept the blessed weeping, saying, "Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh"... And in Job it says, "He will fill the mouth of the truthful with laughter." Perhaps that is why one of the patriarchs is called Laughter. The one, then, who groans [?], as the apostle has shown when he said, "For we who are in this tent groan, being burdened," [longing for] the cheerfulness that is in the promise [?], weeps a weeping that is most nourishing and beneficial to the soul.

We think that "to love" (agapan) is more divine and, so to speak, spiritual, while "to be fond of" (philein) is bodily and more human. Perhaps, since no base person loves in the first sense, we should observe that concerning the better sort it says, "There is none to comfort her among all those who love her," but concerning the lesser: "All who were fond of her have betrayed her; they have become her enemies." For the inferior both betrayed her and became her enemies, while the better merely did not comfort her.

In the literal sense the meaning would be this. Judea exchanged her own place, and the causes of this were her humiliation (into which she was brought by sinning, abandoning the elevation and uprightness she once had when she lived in godliness) and also her great slavery, in which she was enslaved by being subject to the passions. Removed from her home, she settled among the nations, where she could find no rest, since all her enemies pursued her, overtook her and overpowered her, while she was among the nations that afflicted her.

The literal meaning is this. Since the law says, "Three times a year every male of yours shall appear before the Lord your God," the people were eager, once the temple had been built on Zion in the time of Solomon, to carry out the command. And since the cities of Judea lay around Jerusalem, roads led to Zion from every direction. The prophet says that these roads mourn because of the captivity, gloomy and utterly deserted, † even at those seasons when there used to be great gladness and cheer on them, as Jews from everywhere hurried to the feast on Mount Zion. And though many gates had been built in Zion on every side, the text says that all of them have been made desolate, and that the priests could no longer perform [?], either because they had been taken captive or because no one was coming to them and asking for the priestly services. Moreover, it says, the virgins of Zion are being led away, clearly by the enemies who had prevailed.

As to the meaning: since the watching and contemplative faculty is called Zion, there are many roads of the various doctrines, mystical, natural and ethical, and perhaps also logical, that lead to the understanding and contemplation of the matters at hand. When, then, someone loses the practice of these and falls into confusion, all these roads mourn because no one travels them. The roads just mentioned hold festival when they are traveled, examined and, so to speak, traversed; but they mourn when they are deserted, neither searched out nor traveled through, because those who traveled them have fallen away and, taken captive by the passions, have been drawn off toward worse things.
Zion, having nothing sweet at all, lives in bitterness within herself; for "embittered" here is not to be taken as some kind of anger.

The plain sense of the text is something like this. Before the time of the captivity there were some who afflicted the land of Judea, or at least wished to, but they did not prevail, since God shielded the Jews whenever they showed themselves worthy of help. But when the sons of Israel sinned, and not only refused to listen to the prophets but even killed them, then they were handed over into the power of those who afflicted them, so that their enemies became the head, that is, as Symmachus translated, their rulers. Perhaps the enemies are others, distinct from the afflicters, whether in concept or in actual fact. These prospered when those abandoned for their sins became subject to the afflicters. For the Lord humbled the transgressors because of the multitude of their impieties, and did so to such a degree that no mercy was left even for their infants, who went into captivity, driven along by every afflicter.
They ruled and rejoiced because the Lord, for the multitude of their impieties, had handed over to humiliation those who had not kept the covenants with him set down in the holy oracles.

We must clarify the text as far as we are able, examining who the daughter of Zion is, and in what her beauty consists; what the pasture is that the rulers of the daughter of Zion lack, like rams without grazing; and how these, deprived of strength, go before the face of the pursuer. We think that Mount Zion is the mother of the congregation within it, which is called the daughter of Zion, and that the beauty of the daughter of Zion is her property in her robes [?]. This property, seized by the enemies at the time of the plundering, "went out" from those whose adornment it was, that is, was carried off (he used "went out" as the more vivid expression). The leaders of the congregation, since the enemies were pressing upon them and taking them captive, lacked their usual provisions and so were likened to rams that find no food. Just as rams driven along unfed walk feebly, yielding to the compulsion of those who drive them, so too the rulers, having become captives and being led away to the land of their captors, went without strength before the face of the pursuer.

As to the meaning, such a soul is the daughter of Zion. Just as the righteous soul is a daughter of righteousness and the wise soul a child of wisdom, so (since Zion means the watchtower) the soul that keeps watch and contemplatively searches things through might be called the daughter of Zion. What else could I rightly consider her beauty and dignity to be than the wealth of the holy doctrines of truth, contemplated with wisdom? So when someone, after acquiring beauty and dignity, neglects to hold these together and to increase the divine wealth, the things that until then were her adornment flow away and depart. The rulers are those who led in the word and guided her toward the acquisition of that beauty. Like rams, the leaders of a flock of sheep, that find no pasture, they too fell into want, having slackened their attention to the things that could fatten, so to speak, both themselves and the sheep. Therefore, grown weak and overtaken by the pursuer, who is our adversary the devil, they go before him, driven wherever he wishes to lead them. If, however, this daughter of Zion takes care of her beauty and seemliness and takes thought to guard her dignity, she despises and scorns the king of the Assyrians, as we have learned from Isaiah, who says, "The virgin daughter of Zion has despised you and scorned you."
For one who remembers while suffering such things does not remember the present, but the past.
And a little later:

Having raised such difficulties about this passage, and seeking to understand the remembrance of her past humiliation and of her rejections, because her people fell into the hands of the afflicter and the consequences befell her, we consider whether humiliation in the proper sense is not simply sin, just as exaltation is right conduct, and whether rejection comes about through the working of nothing other than wicked action; for this is enough to thrust one away from God and from all that is by nature most beautiful. So when Jerusalem (that is, her inhabitants), drunk and beside herself through sin, was being humiliated, she paid no heed [?] to her faults. But when her retributions came, through her people falling into the hands of the afflicter with no one to help her, then she remembered the things for which she was suffering, perceiving that they were the causes both of her people's fall and of her being left without help.
And a little later:

If such a soul is Jerusalem, it is worth inquiring into her people. When they fall into the hands of the afflicter, since there is no helper, she remembers the days of her humiliation, and also her own rejections by which she was thrust away, and besides these all the desirable things she had from ancient days. Consider whether the people of Jerusalem are not the contemplations in the knowing soul. These fall, cast down by every afflicter, because the soul has become inattentive and negligent. For the doctrines of the negligent flow away, squeezed out by the sins that gain ground in one who neglects better things, and they find no help at all from reason.

The meaning of the text is this. Since Jerusalem sinned a sin, she fell into upheaval and turmoil, so much so that all who had formerly glorified her changed and dishonored that city, having seen her shame. But she, groaning over what she had suffered because of her sins, having fallen into upheaval and into dishonor from those who once glorified her, no longer went forward in her sins, but lessened them and turned back.
And a little later:

If such a soul is called Jerusalem, one that is quick and discerning and able to contemplate the peace of God that surpasses all "understanding," then, since she can sin for many reasons, the text shows that she has fallen into upheaval, having departed from good things and come to be among worse ones. For everyone who has fallen from virtue and lives with vice is rightly said to be in upheaval.
It shows that Jerusalem's sins have been checked: she no longer "strains forward to what lies ahead" in her faults, nor is she engaged in sins, but she turns back toward her own good.

According to the bodily account, what is now said about Jerusalem is this. The uncleanness of Jerusalem is a hindrance; but the prophet has left it to us to work out what it hinders. Perhaps, then, it shows that the uncleanness hinders her course. But, being of this kind, it also shows that Jerusalem did not remember her last end. Whoever keeps this before his eyes and sees what will befall him because of his sins will not sin. Because of this uncleanness, then, she is hindered; and because she did not remember her last end, he brought down her wonderful and great things, which she had when she was worthy to be watched over, and reduced them to lowliness, though formerly they were exceedingly great and beyond all praise. Yet even after all this there was no one to comfort her who [?] her greatest things [?]. "Consider, Lord, the humiliation of me who speak, since the enemy is magnified over what has happened to my homeland."
And a little later:

We must inquire, however, according to the rules of anagogy, whether uncleanness can be present in someone who is not its cause [?]. Let us also look at the first ideas of the Lament. Such a soul, having fallen, is certainly also in uncleanness, and this uncleanness prevents her from traveling the holy road. The holy Moses, and his successor Joshua, are commanded by God to take off their sandals when stepping on holy ground, since it is not fitting to have dead hide around one's feet in a holy place. Just so, if anyone is to travel without hindrance, he must perhaps not only take off his shoes but also wash off the uncleanness that has come upon his feet from the dust. We think that a symbol of this is the Savior's pouring water into the basin and washing his disciples' feet, saying to Peter, who did not yet understand the mystery and therefore tried to stop him, "Unless I wash you, you have no part with me," and "What I am doing you do not know now, but you will know afterward." So it will be necessary, regarding the uncleanness on what we may call the feet of the soul, to ask Jesus to wash it off, so that we may be able to have a part with him. For if it remains, it hinders us from walking the road in accordance with sound reason, that is, the Savior, who said, "I am the way."

It is clear that the healthy soul, or at least the soul that wishes to be such, does these things, looking not so much at the present alone as foreseeing what will meet it in the future as a result of what it does. If, when something seemingly good is happening in the present, it foresees bitterness in the future, it dismisses what seems sweet and does the opposite, so as not to fall into some hardship afterward. But if the present is toilsome, and good hopes follow what appears harsh, it will willingly give itself up to the roughness of what some would think terrible, in order to obtain the sweet things that follow the harsh ones for those who have endured them.

Having suffered all these things, he says, the one called Jerusalem in a more figurative sense found no one to comfort her. For having turned away from the reason within her and become wholly given over to passion, she lost her helper, the one who always arms the disposition that attends to him against toils and against things thought terrible. On top of this, "see the humiliation of me, the citizen," as a kindred of the soul might say: "The suffering of my fellow citizen is my own misfortune, because of the love for humanity I have been taught. Consider, then, O Lord, and do not utterly abandon her who has suffered these things. Do not overlook the enemy that is against her," meaning vice, which has grown great and poured itself out against her. "See, Lord, my humiliation" can also be taken more figuratively as spoken by the reason dwelling in the soul, which has been dishonored and humbled and has, so to speak, lost its own kingdom.

The desirable things of Jerusalem, then, are to be understood as the things in the temple: the holy things of the holy of holies, set apart for the priestly service [?], and the things otherwise believed to be divine because they were kept in the temple, such as the golden lampstand and the rest. For the people, convinced that these were kept in the temple for the glory of God, valued them above everything, wishing rather to suffer some grievous thing themselves at the hands of the enemy than that any of these should fall into the enemies' hands. And those of the circumcision are accustomed to call the temple "the sanctuary."

At the time of the captivity Jerusalem suffered something most extraordinary. For she saw nations, which God had commanded not to enter the assembly, trampling the sanctuary, where it was not lawful even for Israelites to enter. Only the priests were deemed worthy to be in that place, and only after no ordinary purifications. The enemies went so far as to enter even the inaccessible places, into the place which the high priest "entered once a year," and barely, "with much sanctification."
And shortly afterward:

If, as we have already shown, Jerusalem is such a soul, then her natural goods should be understood as her adornment, by which she served God. They were stored in her inner places, which no one may enter except the high-priestly Word, and these are called her desirable things. The enemy who had prevailed in the wrestling match stretched out his hand over all of these. He afflicted the soul that had not fought well on her own behalf and had been justly abandoned by divine help. Extending himself through his power, which is so active for evil, he tore them away from her ruling faculty and left the soul that had turned away from God bare of good things. In this passage the nations should also be taken allegorically as the crowd of vices that entered the ruling faculty, which was created to make room for God and to be a true sanctuary for him who wishes to rest in a pure mind. God altogether forbids these nations to enter the assembly. For what should we think God forbids more strictly to enter a soul counted in the assembly of God than the works and the mind of the flesh, which are truly nations hostile to God? "For the flesh wars against the Spirit," since "the mind of the flesh is hostile to God; for it does not submit to God's law, nor indeed can it."

They groaned because of famine, and for a little food that would restore their failing life they gave up their most precious things. But how could they offer the desirable things mentioned earlier in exchange for food, if the enemy had carried them off? The answer is that "the enemy stretched out his hand over everything," but once he had his fill of taking what he wanted, he left the rest behind. It was with these that they bought food.

"See, Lord, my disgrace" is a prayer from Jerusalem, who has lost her adornment because of famine. Perhaps, though, there are two kinds of desirable things. The first are those already described, "over which the enemy stretched out his hand [?]"; the second are the possessions of each individual among the people. The enemy took the common treasures, and each person bought food with his private belongings. To give the higher meaning: Esau sold his birthright for red food, and from it he took the name Edom, that is, "red earth." For he became earthly, since he despised the birthright and gave first place to earthly things. Jacob pursued those same things as necessities, but only in a secondary way, because he was in a body. Jerusalem did the same as Esau. But Esau gave the desirable things he had to Jacob, who was worthy to receive them, even though he had not preferred them. The people of Jerusalem also gave theirs for the sake of food, but the food was not prepared by a holy man. It came from Babylonians, who were going to treat the desirable things they received with contempt. For Jacob knew how to put what he received from Esau to good use, but the Babylonians do not use what is given them for their own good. In the same way, a soul that lacks what it needs throws away the divine teachings to those who want to learn them out of idle curiosity, for slander and mockery.

He has described the fire that broke out at the capture of the city and seized the strongest buildings. Or he means the capture of her most eminent citizens, who were set on fire, as it were, by their calamities, both in their souls and in their outward circumstances. He also describes how the lower classes were caught for slavery, as if in a hunt with nets, because they had not used their freedom well. For these people were not straining forward to what lies ahead [?] what lies behind. Instead they turned back from glory to dishonor and from freedom to slavery. Instead of being honored, they were darkened and obscured by dishonor and outrage. For this reason the city fell into unending grief.

"Providence," she says, "has not slept over my sins. God took them, as it were, into his hands, examined them, and wove them together with the deeds that bring requital. They have become like a yoke on my neck, and he has laid slavery upon me. The slavery in which I served Nebuchadnezzar is my own sins. That is why I have grown weak, since I have been handed over to those whose rule I cannot endure."
And shortly afterward:

"His yoke is upon my neck." This passage shows that the things said about God as though he had passions like ours must be understood figuratively. How else could the sins of Jerusalem be woven together by the hand of God, except figuratively? No one would claim that this too is meant in a bodily sense. And would it not be absurd to take the neck figuratively, since Jerusalem is a city, but not to understand the limbs ascribed to God in the same way? Let these words now be taken as spoken by a soul that has fallen asleep in ungodliness. It has thrown off the saving yoke of sound reason, which the Savior calls easy, and has put on the yoke of sins. Because of them it has grown weak, since it has been abandoned by God's oversight and handed over to sin, which reigns over evils. Because wickedness has no limit or end, the soul cannot fully serve sin's wishes or ever satisfy it. Sin truly humbles a person, chokes him, and makes him look down. Conscience is also a yoke: it is always choking and wounding, does not allow one to lift up one's head, and takes away all freedom of speech. "And it has paralyzed," she says, "even the strength that I did not use well, and I am undone as I look upon the evils that hold me fast."

He did not remove them from my midst (for even if I had been deprived of them, it would still have been possible to make use of them for other purposes). Rather, he condemned them to suffer in my midst because of my impieties, and my chosen ones have suffered the harshest things, since the Lord himself trod the wine of his wrath in the winepress until I was sated with it, I and the virgin of most royal Judah. By "mighty ones" he would mean those who are powerful in war and defend their homeland, and by "chosen ones" the noble or the wise. The words "trod the winepress" are explained by what is said in the Psalms about the punishment of sinners: "A cup in the hand of the Lord, full of a mixture of unmixed wine." It is tipped from this one who is being punished to that one who is being punished, until "all the sinners of the earth" drink. The dregs are left for those who are still more sinful than these, and on them, last of all, "the dregs" will be emptied out.

It is not hard to see how the Lord trod the winepress for the virgin daughter of Judah. Since "whatever each one sows, that he will also reap," perhaps whatever he cultivates is also what he harvests. So the one who has made better wine will rejoice in his own produce. But the one who has cultivated the vine of Sodom and the vine-shoot of Gomorrah, and has borne a grape of gall, a cluster of bitterness and the incurable wrath of asps, will drink what matches such fruits. All of it is gathered by the Lord into one winepress, and his evil works are trodden and pressed out, so that he will drink until he vomits up the gall, the bitterness and the wrath. He will drink, according to Jeremiah, so as to vomit, but according to Isaiah, so as to be roused and to put on the glory that is proper to him. For the Lord does not tread the winepress in vain, and least of all for the virgin daughter of Judah.

So the soul had received many mighty and choice gifts from the one who created it. Deprived of them through wickedness and paying the penalty, it confesses what it has suffered. The "time" that was called "to crush" is the time of retribution, when, according to Ezekiel, "none of the righteous deeds that the righteous man has done will be remembered in the day of his sin." Yet by mourning over what has happened, the soul is helped, for those who mourn and weep have the promise of comfort and of laughter.

He said that the cause of the lamentations is that there is no one to restore her soul, or, according to Symmachus, no one to recover it. He also says that her sons have been destroyed, because the enemy grew strong through the sins they committed. When we live piously, the enemy has no strength. He weakens as we make progress and is put to death as we are made perfect, and he is crushed underfoot, "ground fine like dust before the wind" and "ground like the mud of the streets." He feeds and gains strength in proportion to our sins, but when we have stopped transgressing he wastes away as if from hunger. Conversely, by doing good we strengthen the divine powers on our side, and by sinning we drive them away. That is why Symmachus rendered "desolate" instead of "destroyed." A contemplative soul might say these things when through negligence it has lost this gladdening word of truth, together with all its fruits, which are called its sons, because wickedness, its enemy, has grown strong against it.

By Zion he means the mountain, by Jacob the people, and by Jerusalem the capital city. God gave Jacob commandments, and because these were transgressed he was surrounded by enemies. But according to Symmachus and another edition of the Seventy, the Lord commanded that those who oppressed him should be all around him, that is, the powers appointed to do harm.

He has shown Jerusalem's uncleanness through sin by the image of a menstruous woman. By "among them" he means either between Zion and Jacob, or in the middle of the whole mountain (for the city was built on part of it) and of the whole people, with Jacob here meaning the twelve tribes. Taken literally, Zion and Jerusalem can be understood in two ways: either as the places or as their inhabitants. If Zion is a place, he says that her hands, that is, her works, such as farming and anything made by hand, are spread out and not drawn in, and are not doing the work proper to hands, as happens in an idle and deserted land. But if he means the inhabitants, the hands would be the farmers and workers, who do not put their hands to work because of the circumstances that surround them. And if Zion's hands are taken figuratively, how much more must the limbs that Scripture ascribes to God be taken that way! The mountain itself, so to speak, groans together with the nation, having neither God nor any holy man to console it.

"The mouth of the Lord" must be understood as the prophets. Isaiah was one of them, and he said, "For the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things." Jerusalem was reproached by the Savior as the one who "killed the prophets," and in that sense she embittered the mouth of the Lord by handing them over to the bitterest sufferings. God, who requires the blood of the prophets, hands over her young men and virgins to the captivities that follow wars, again and again. So, in return for what she has suffered, she makes confession before the others and offers herself to them as an example, so that they may learn God's righteousness and not suffer the same things.
Beyond the literal sense, understand "virgins" as those who live in incorruption, and "young men" as those who are approved in virtue. For the saints often suffer along with the guilty.

Ezekiel has shown who the lovers are when he says to Jerusalem, whom he calls Oholibah: "Thus says the Lord, the Lord: Behold, I am stirring up your lovers against you from every side, the sons of Babylon and all the Chaldeans." These had formerly been friends, but by divine providence they turned to enmity. This often happens when love turns into hatred. For he says about Samaria: "And Oholah played the harlot away from me and set her desire on her lovers, the Assyrians," and a little later: "Therefore I handed her over into the hands of her lovers, into the hands of the sons of the Assyrians." He also says about Jerusalem: "And her sister Oholibah saw, and she was more corrupt in her desire than her sister in her harlotry, and she set her desire on the sons of the Assyrians."

In the prophecy, then, he is pained in soul as one who is about to suffer the most terrible things. In the present Lament, however, as if these things had already happened, she is grieved and confesses that through her sins she has bitterly provoked the kindness of God, so that she who had many children has been bereaved of them, and, most terrible of all, by an enemy's hand. Since this is personification, one should not look for a city's womb that bore children or a heart that has been broken.

Jerusalem divides her speech between the enemies, whom she wants to hear her, and God. But why does she call on her enemies to listen? And why does she tell God that they rejoiced? Perhaps it is this: through her trespass and Israel's, salvation has come to the Gentiles to make Israel jealous, and when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, then all Israel will be saved. So she speaks the first words prophetically to those from among the Gentiles, and the second to God: "I was left to suffer so that you might gain a place, and because of you I became an enemy of God, although as regards election I am beloved for the sake of the fathers. So when you have heard my groaning, [?] understand also its cause. I have been utterly forsaken for the sake of your salvation, and I no longer have the one who always consoled me after I had experienced evils. For now a ruler has failed from Judah, and a leader from his loins. He for whom these things were reserved has come, the expectation of the [?]; and since his blood is being avenged, there is no longer anyone to comfort Jerusalem."

That is: let their wickedness no longer be allowed free play, but let it come under your oversight, as if someone were to pray that his wounds might come under a physician's eye so that he might obtain complete healing. This is the sense of "all." For the most blessed thing is not to sin at all, and the second is that all our wickedness should be examined by God.

To glean is to gather, after the vintage, the small remnants that have been left, which is what the poor do. So it is as if she says: "When you watched over me carefully, you cleansed my branches, removing everything inferior, down to the smallest bits, of the grape [?] and of the cluster of bitterness. In the same way, glean my enemies. This is to my benefit, if indeed, after they have been completely saved, I too, by your judgment, O Lord, shall obtain salvation. When I see them, I am deeply grieved and I condemn myself, since I need your oversight."

David has a similar saying: "He will break all the horns of sinners." Here he means the rulers, in whom the strength of the nation lies, as strength lies in the horns of horned animals; and also because the horn stands out from the body as rulers stand out from their subjects. Daniel too likened kingdoms to horns. The horn also signifies the arrogance of the ruling part of the soul, as in "Do not lift up your horn on high." So by turning away his saving hand, God made them easy prey for the enemies, whom he called an all-consuming flame. You might also call every lofty thought a horn, and the "passions of dishonor," to which the transgressor is handed over, a fire. Such a person has lost all the help that surrounded him, as in "The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him."

The enemies even dared to commit slaughter in the temple, with God's permission. "Like an enemy" is well said, for God does not punish out of enmity. He does it because he wants to benefit either those who suffer or those who look on. He calls the temple a "tent" after the sanctuary that existed from the beginning, and he calls his punishing power a "bow," as in Habakkuk: "You will surely bend your bow against the scepters, says the Lord." These scepters are clearly the hostile principalities and powers. The Son, who is the right hand of God the Father, fought them down completely [?]. He overthrew the idols they had set up in the temple of God (for these are the "desire of the eyes"), and in place of the idols he killed the demons that had made their dwelling in them.

By "palaces" he means the houses, which Symmachus rendered "royal residences." He repeats the laments, as someone in deep pain would in mourning. Again he shows that she has taken on a humbled way of reasoning and a humbled mind, now that what were, as it were, her dwellings and fortresses have been torn down, the things that, as it were, filled her ruling faculty. The dwellings are the virtues, since they shelter us, and the strongholds are the reasonings that cannot be refuted. For this is not the tearing down of evil "high things raised up against the knowledge of God," nor the humility by which one "learns the statutes of God." Those would be reasons for joy, but this is not.

By "tent" he means the temple, and by "vine" and "vineyard" Israel, as in David, "You brought a vine out of Egypt," and in Isaiah, "My beloved had a vineyard." David goes on, "Why have you broken down its hedge?" and so on, and Isaiah, "You have taken away its hedge," and what follows. The present Lament has shown the same things. God withdrew his guard and handed it over to the enemies, with [?] no longer encamping around it, because it did not fear the [?]. He also abolished the times the law appointed for worship, as he says in Isaiah: "Your fasting and rest and your feasts my soul hates." This he called forgetting, though not as a human weakness. And he provoked king and priest, who were indignant that, though they were God's portion, they were suffering such things at the hands of the impious.

He handed over the vessels used in worship, since he was no longer pleased with the sacrifices of the impious, as in "Burnt offerings of rams, and the fat of lambs, and the blood of bulls and goats I do not want." He also handed over the wall that enclosed the houses of the city, or the royal residences, as Symmachus rendered it. And the enemies, having taken even the temple, celebrated with shouting as if they had won a complete victory. The soul's altar is the rational part within us, through which the passions are put to death and offered as a sacrifice.
For he took away all her security and stretched out the measure of her punishment. Zechariah also saw this.

The wall and the outer wall mourn. They are things worthy of mourning, and they make even those who look at them weep. "For who will scatter the counsel of the Lord? And who will turn back his uplifted hand?" as the blessed Isaiah says. She mourns over such things, whether she is a city or a soul, so that she has become something for the enemies to trample. It is fitting, then, that the angels who formerly guarded her, one after another, greater and lesser, should mourn for her. For if they rejoice over those who are saved, how will they not mourn over those who have fallen?

For they vanished as if swallowed up by land or sea. King, rulers and false prophets perished, and so did her law, under the constraint of slavery, though they had already abolished it by their own choice even before they were captured. The gates of the soul are the senses. When the soul sins, they are flooded with passions and become earthly. And the powers of the soul that guard them grow slack once the reigning mind and the ruling thoughts have perished in the passions. Then the soul's law and order are destroyed, and it becomes Babylon, full of confusion, with no provident power helped by God.

He describes painful sights that took place in the very place of gladness. Out of fear, the elders were not even allowed to lament, and the leading virgins were made to keep their eyes on the ground, so that they would not be seen and, by the beauty in which they excelled, draw the enemies to violence. You might also say this of those who were once elders in virtue, which is why they were called elders. They have become earthly and settled in irrational passions, so that they no longer do anything according to reason. They have made the ruling spirit within them earthly, turned the chastity they once had into something to be mourned, and corrupted the thoughts they had previously kept uncorrupted.

By "his own glory" the prophet means the temple of God and the piety of his homeland. It was famine that made the infants faint. In a loftier sense, you might say that he makes the sufferings of his kinsmen according to the flesh his own, as in "Who is weak, and I am not weak?" He takes on himself the hardships of their souls: the withering of true knowledge, the unsteady drift of reason toward earthly things, and the loss of the one who lifts up the head, as in "You, Lord, are my helper, my glory, and the one who lifts up my head."

He has shown utter wickedness, such that there is no testimony to any virtue, nor anyone who has transgressed in the same way. For what sin is like that of one who rebelled against God, not from far off, but after having drawn near to him? "If I had not come," he says, "and spoken to them, they would not have sin." That is why it is said, "Among those who draw near to me I will be sanctified," since "the one who does not know the will of the Lord and does not do it will receive few blows, but the one who knows it and does not do it will receive many." So such great suffering, which the prophets were unable to heal, needs God alone. That is why he also took on flesh, while the prophets confessed their weakness in the words "Lord, who has believed our report?" Jerusalem also said earlier, "See if there is any suffering like my suffering." The one who struck, then, will heal, for he causes pain and restores again. The word "who" is used both of something rare and of no one at all, for no human being can heal a blow inflicted by God.

A vain prophecy is one that has no fulfillment, and one that vain idols produce. Some also prophesied on their own authority, supposedly, "for a handful of barley and a scrap of bread," as it is written. They do not know how to expose sins and rescue people from captivity to the demons, and they pervert souls with smooth talk. The oracle and the word that true prophets receive from God are true and join one to God. In the same way, the oracle of the demons is false and puts one far from God, and drives one away from the help that comes from him. What, then, are the expulsions and oracles that are not vain, as has been shown? Clearly, those that drive one out of error and bring one to God.

For "our enemy the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to swallow," and like a serpent he lets out his hissing against us. But may he never say, "We have swallowed her up," nor find in us the day that the scorching sun brings about. For it is said, "The sun will not scorch you by day." He scorches with pleasures and anger, and offers error as though it were light and knowledge. So we will sing the psalm: "If it had not been that the Lord was among us [?], they would have swallowed us alive," and also, "The lamp of the ungodly will be put out."

The enemies, he says, did nothing of their own accord. It seemed good to God, and it came to pass. That is why Nebuzaradan also said: "The Lord your God spoke these evils against this place, and the Lord brought them about, because you sinned against him." So everyone who doubts the judgment will hear it in these words. All the prophets foretold these things, but from days of old Moses announced them in Deuteronomy.

Sometimes Scripture fills its words with emotion and gives feeling to things that have none. It presents hills leaping and mountains skipping, and calls hills and stones as witnesses. But that is impossible here, since the wall had already been torn down by the enemies. Here, then, the wall is the king, the rulers, and all who by their power wall the city around. She asks them to shed unceasing tears of repentance, the kind of tears that the fallen wall continually draws from those who see it. These things, he says, apply to them. Otherwise it signifies once more the grief of the power that formerly guarded her, expressed in hyperbole. "In affliction," it says, "they remembered the Lord with their whole heart." So do this, he says: weep night and day, and "be pierced with sorrow upon your beds." Do not think that release from these tears is sobriety, for repentance leads to salvation. A person becomes sober by ceasing from what is worse, not from what is good. Join yourself in mind to Christ at all times, so that he may guard you like the pupil of his eye and become a wall for you.

Night favors attentiveness, since the soul gathers itself in when the senses are still. That is when it bids us meditate on God's commandments and say with David: "By night I communed with my heart, and my spirit searched." And since the night is divided into four watches, say with David, "My eyes were awake before the watches," and with Habakkuk, "I will stand at my watch and look out to see what the Lord God will speak in me." For then you will say, "that he will speak peace to his people." So meditate in the night of this present age, for your "struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against the principalities, against the powers." "For you do not know when the master of the house is coming, in the evening, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or in the morning. Otherwise he may come suddenly and find you asleep." And again: "For if you had known in which watch the thief was coming, you would have stayed awake and would not have let your house be broken into."

Lift up your hands to him by doing good works. This struggle is not about trivial things. Your infants are fainting for lack of the divine word. They stand at the head of all the ways out, which are God's commandments, and they cannot go forward without God's help and the bread that strengthens the heart.

After the prophet's exhortation, Jerusalem was persuaded and says to God: "Do not turn your face away from me," "Look upon me and have mercy on me," "Do not rebuke me in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath." "The blow is greater than human nature can bear. I know that I transgressed the law and incurred the penalties it lays down, among them, 'You will eat the offspring of your womb, the flesh of your sons and daughters.' I thought those words were only a threat; but, Lord, 'your law is truth.' Yet I was never told of the slaughter of priest and prophet in the middle of the temple."

All those who were too young or too old for hard labor lay thrown on the ground, a most pitiful sight, as was the slaughter of young men and virgins [?]. Would that these too had been slaughtered before they were led away to a more bitter life! The "streets" of the earth are the affairs of this life. In them they fell asleep, "neither keeping watch nor praying," and through folly [?] they closed the eyes of their souls. Who are these people? If they are children, it is not very surprising. But as it is, before them those who seemed to have advanced in virtue, and everyone who was uncorrupted in soul and mighty in war, have fallen into the enemies' hands. You, being good, put an end to such a life of theirs and cut down every alliance they formed for evil.

"Those around me who lived in Judea," she says, "regarded the feast held in me as a refuge and hoped for salvation from it. None of them is left, because of the wrath you brought on them. For through their sins the enemies became many and strong."

Terrible things happened to the prophet both before the city was captured and after its capture. So, as he begins another alphabetic sequence, he laments over himself, seeing the poverty and desolation of the city brought about by the Lord's chastisement. He himself was no less in want of good things. He was in distress when he was rebuking them, so that he says, "I have been mocked all day long," and at the same time he shared in the misfortunes of their calamities and in the [?] that comes from sympathy. He also says, as David did, "The shadow of death overshadowed me." For whenever God seems to give a brief respite from the sufferings, he turns back again and makes the punishment continual.

"All day" means every day, as in David: "Fighting all day long, he afflicted me." "He turned his hand" might also mean that he who formerly supplied me with good things now brings chastisements, as though he had changed hands.
He means the decay that came upon us from sin.
For prolonged misfortune brings on the weakness of old age.

For he did not let me escape the terrors, since I was besieged on every side. Perhaps he also means the hostile wall thrown around the city. He has said the same as David, who said, "They have made me sit in dark places like those long dead." He says this because of the enemies' prisons, and also because of the calamities that come from God, for trials are darkness to the soul. In particular he means "the [?] into which Pashhur threw Jeremiah," which was dark and without light, just like the cave in which David hid from Saul. These two Lamentations could also be taken as referring to Christ. Jeremiah was a type of him, since he suffered so much at the hands of the Jews and was finally handed over to a tomb.

He has surrounded me with evils I cannot escape. He has laid on my neck a harsh and provoking people, a burden too heavy for me. Though I often prayed to be relieved, I was not heard, for sometimes circumstances prevent even the saints from being heard. By "yoke" he might also mean the iron collars that he put on at God's command in place of the wooden ones. In fact, there is also a reading: "For he made the bronze of my neck heavy." For he shut out my prayer, saying to him also: "Do not pray for them, for I will not hear you."

Though he often set out to give up his ministry, he was not allowed to. He said, "I will not name the name of the Lord," and yet he was driven on as if by fire. God also blocks the ways of sinners by not allowing them to sin. But the prophet is not one of these, for he says, "I did not sit in the council of those who make merry."
He has emptied every arrow of his against me, he says, wounding my desire and not allowing me to act as I wish.

In Scripture the "kidneys" stand for the faculty of desire, and the "darts" are the arrows. "And then they mocked me as a liar, making me their song." Earlier he had said, "I sat alone, because I was filled with bitterness," and what follows. For he was praying for them while they were plotting against him, and yet he could not give up his ministry. So he was embittered: he suffered at their hands, he grieved with them in their sufferings, and he was deeply distressed at their impiety.

"With gravel," he says, or "one by one," as each tooth is struck against the jaw, or else with a hard stone. Like David he also says, "I ate ashes as my bread," showing that because of his affliction he could not take even bread with any pleasure. So the soul could not be at peace. It was troubled in itself, and it also saw tumults without and battles within. "Therefore, hoping for nothing good, I uttered cries like Job's: 'Mercy has renounced me, and so has my hope from the Lord.'" For it was not possible to overcome the dangers that surrounded him.

For he is good to all, but he requires endurance from us. For the soul that will seek him, the seeking is good. Such a soul would wait without being troubled until mercy came to meet it, and would not shift its hope to another until the salvation of the Lord appeared. Perhaps by "will keep quiet" he means not prying into the judgments of providence. So even when we do not understand, we must not throw off the Lord's reins.

Because "his yoke is easy and his burden light." If no one agrees with him about something, he must not be carried along with them. Even if he is left alone in it, he must hold fast to what he has resolved and stand firmly settled in it. For "the Lord settles the solitary in a house," says David, and "I am alone until I pass by," meaning, clearly, until I pass by the trials, having received loving-kindness.

For he will humble himself, saying, "I am earth and ashes," if he is truly a man, and he is filled with the hope that does not put to shame. This is like the words "My soul has cleaved to the ground."

This also fits those in captivity who speak the words of the seventy-third Psalm: "Why, O God, have you rejected us forever? Has your anger blazed against the sheep of your pasture?" The words "The Lord will not reject forever, nor will he be angry for all ages" agree with it. And to the one who has repented as he ought, he will say, "Let your voice cease from weeping, and your eyes from tears."

From these words we learn that the Lord did not command the humbling of the earth's prisoners by sin, nor is he its cause. Nor is he the cause of human judgments being perverted before God, for God loves what is just and right. Nor is he the cause of its being thought proper to condemn a man. For opposites, he says, cannot come out of the mouth of the Lord, both good things and evil. A [good] tree does not bear bad fruit, and a bad tree does not bear good fruit. So when people are wronged by the wicked, this is against God's judgment. Yet it happens among those whom God overlooks, as it happened to the Israelites at the hands of their enemies, and it comes to an end when God turns back to them. Therefore those handed over to punishment must seek that turning.

So it is in vain that we grumble and lay the blame on the Creator. The living man has no business doing this, for such a disposition belongs to those who are dead in sins. Or perhaps he is reproving the one who lives in sin and also blames God. Since, then, we have no one else to blame but ourselves, let us judge what we ourselves have done and turn back.

For no one who does not know himself can return to the Lord. A person comes to know himself by applying his mind to his actions, at once examining them and making them spiritual. For then "with unveiled face we behold the glory of the Lord as in a mirror," and, confessing our former deeds, we shall say, "We have sinned and turned away from you," and, "You are just in all that you have brought upon us."
"Lifting up our hearts upon our hands" seems to mean that we should, as it were, take our own thoughts into our hands and examine whether they are pure.

This too is part of the confession already begun. You brought upon us the press of calamities like darkness out of a cloud. You pursued us when we were far from you, and through punishment you destroyed us who were dead in sin. Our sins separated us from you like a cloud walling us off, and so our prayer did not reach you. For we did not have "the wings of a dove" to fly over and say, "In my God I shall leap over a wall." It was not easy to get past sin, for it is solid and dark and has no share in the Holy Spirit.

Symmachus has "terror." They swallowed us with their whole mouth, and we were carried down into a depth of evils, filled with fear and confusion. For "the sinner falls into the pit he dug," paying the penalty for his sins. And since, according to Solomon, "insolence," that is, arrogance, "goes before ruin," we were lifted up and then crushed. That is why David sings, "Let not the foot of pride come against me, and let not the hand of the sinner shake me."
Though he has suffered so much, he grieves deeply for those who did it. So true is it that "love keeps no account of wrong."

In place of "My eye was worn out, and will not be silent, so that there is no sobering," Symmachus said, "My eye persisted and did not stop, so that there is no relief." The Seventy show that although his eyes had grown weak from so many tears, he still did not stop, since he could not come to himself from his weeping. Symmachus shows that "I persisted in tears and did not stop." For earnest prayer and intense weeping draw God to mercy.

For tears cut me down, he says, as a thorough harvester strips a vine. According to Symmachus, "tears drowned me," a metaphor taken from those who are choked in water. "Patiently I shall wait for the Lord as long as he keeps his face turned away from us." God's "looking down" means his counting us worthy of his visitation. He explains "beyond all" by putting "over all" instead, that is, over their misfortunes, for the female sex is more pitiable than the male.

Or he is speaking of what he himself suffered. He was thrown into a pit and came close to dying, but was saved beyond hope, and could say with David, "My soul was rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters." For, as the Savior said, it was not possible "to fall to the ground without the Father who is in [heaven]." So he is speaking either of himself or as one who makes the people's sufferings his own. But "without cause" could fittingly be said of him. For what wrong had he done them? Or rather, what good had he not done them?

God gave judgment by killing the false prophet and handing over the king, and, in the case of Christ, by handing over the nation to capture. The words "I before their eyes" mean that I was a burden to them even to look at.

He also said earlier, "Make an end of them, and your word will be to me gladness and the joy of my heart." These things came after the plot against the Savior, when they were scattered everywhere, for "all the righteous [blood]" came upon them. So [?] signifies that their worship came to an end and that they are no longer called God's nation.

"A shield of heart, toil for them" means that you will give them toil so that they come to perceive how great a shield you had been for them, and may seek you again. If they do not, you will pursue them in your anger.
Beginning the present fourth alphabetic poem, he takes up again the lament over the eminent in particular. He says that their splendor has grown dim and has vanished like water poured out.
They are "holy" as being chosen, either because of the fathers or because of the saints taken captive with Jehoiakim, whom he likened to good figs.
And a little later:

By "exits" he means those that lead away from the holy land into [?] and into the spiritual Babylonian, "that they may be taught not to blaspheme." You could also apply the Lament to those who turn away from piety, if they were prominent and led others into error, "having forsaken the fountain of living water, and become broken cisterns that cannot hold water." So they are fittingly poured out into error, groaning before their time.

Those who prided themselves on wealth, he says, or who were even more precious than gold — how were they led away into slavery and likened to cheap, breakable things? He also said that they were likened to these when he went down "to the potter's house" and took a vessel [?] them; and Isaiah likens them to a fallen city: "and its ruins will be like the fragments of a vessel."

He speaks of the famine of the noble infants: Jerusalem could not even offer them the breast as wild animals do. Extreme suffering makes people forget even nature. By the "dragons," or by Symmachus's "Sirens," you will understand the evil spirits, which suckled their own young with evil milk. Such are those who are initiated into the teachings of the impious.

For how are those who have become effeminate not "daughters"? Pharaoh too keeps them alive while killing the males. They graze over the teaching, God's wilderness, but like ostriches they cannot fly away and are forever running about on the earth. For this is how Symmachus rendered the "sparrow," and he quite fittingly called their teachers Sirens. For in the pagan myth the Sirens destroyed those who came upon them through pleasure, just as dragons do by biting with their venom. So he reproaches the supposedly good teachers because they did not take even as much care for their pupils as these creatures do.

They suffered these things when they were besieged and led away. You could also say that, in the prophet's words, "they endured a famine not of bread, nor of water, but of hearing the word of the Lord." That is why he prophesies about their infants.
Historically he has returned to what happened during the captivity, but in its deeper sense he is speaking of the famine of the teaching word.

For the poor who are ill-treated are not so pitiable. Paul too laments these people, saying, "to whom belong the adoption and the glory." For now they study empty things and do not delight in Moses and the prophets, as in "Delight in the Lord." There is no one to bake the nourishing word for them, and they do not share in the fatted calf, though they themselves sacrificed it. By "exits" he means the dispersions, or else the distortions of the writings of the law.
Formerly they were nursed on scarlet, hearing beforehand through prophecy of the Saviour's blood that was to be shed; now they are clothed in the rags of earthly notions.

Symmachus rendered "as in haste" as "suddenly," and "they did not labour" as "which they did not wound." For what is swifter than the divine word, which said, "Behold, your house is left to you desolate," and handed it over by will alone? The iniquity of Jerusalem grew greater than that of Sodom. The people of Sodom had only the natural law, but these had the written law as well, and the prophets, and all the wonders God worked among them. And the people of Sodom sinned against angels and against men like themselves, but these sinned against the Saviour and Redeemer, who of old redeemed them from Egypt and now would have redeemed them from the worship of demons, had they received him who came to them first. For he says, "I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel."

Symmachus: "Her separated ones were spotless as snow, brighter than milk, ruddier in complexion than precious things, their limbs sapphire; their appearance is darker than soot." He means those who consecrated themselves to God, for "Nazirites" signifies "consecrated ones." That is how Symmachus and Theodotion rendered "Nazirites" in Amos, as "consecrated ones." Moses also mentions them, and Samson was one of them. They were also held in honour among the Jews. So he compared their purity to snow and their brightness to milk. They were made fiery by their discipline, having been proved in what they had promised to God; and their chosen ones (which is what "their cutting" means) lead a heavenly way of life, for such is the colour of sapphire. Sapphire also has golden veins, and Symmachus likens their condition to these, since it is incorruptible and glows with the fire of piety.

They fell away from spiritual illumination and wasted away in the spiritual famine, so that they resembled dry wood "not planted by the streams of water." Such now are their priests, having [no?] spiritual nourishment. And in the literal sense, their faces were blackened with utter shame because they were led away like the others, having sinned as they did; for even now ordinary usage applies the word to those who are put to shame.

For it is better to die quickly in war than to be worn down by famine for lack of the produce of the field. You could say that the sword and the blade are the word of God, for Paul says, "and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God." By it, the bride says, "I am wounded with love." And David says, "Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one, in your comeliness and your beauty." Those struck by such a sword should fall at the feet of Jesus, as in "peoples will fall beneath you," confessing his kingdom, rather than be overtaken by famine of the soul. For Christ is the produce of the land, born in Bethlehem, which means "House of Bread." Because the Jews had no taste of him, they were led away into the land of demons. And the field blessed by the Lord and very fragrant, whose fragrance Jacob breathed, signifies the church of Christ.

So that the women may not seem to have eaten their children out of cruelty, he says that they were compassionate and attributes the deed to the compulsion of want. "They boiled" means kindling a fire and cooking, which did indeed happen in the Roman siege. That is why he also calls the complete ruin of the nation "destruction." He mentions this same suffering in the second alphabet of Lamentations too. Josephus also recorded this and the other sufferings accurately in his work on the capture of Jerusalem.
For these things were fulfilled after the coming of Christ.

Perhaps this was also because of the strength of the place and its wall and the might of its inhabitants, but chiefly because of God, who had always defended the city. And yet before Nebuchadnezzar the Egyptian had often entered and taken the treasures from the house of the Lord, but he did not sack the city. Though he was an enemy, he did not press it very hard, so it was not out of keeping that the marvel should happen twice or three times. He could also mean by "kings of the earth" the demons who ruled over the earthly, of whom it is said, "All the kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ." Who they are is shown by "For if they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory," and by "that the manifold wisdom of God might be made known through the church to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places." For they thought that Jerusalem would never be handed over completely, supposing that the promise to the fathers was limited to this nation, since they knew nothing about Christ.
Righteous blood is properly that of Christ the Saviour. By shedding it they perished utterly, whereas for the blood of the prophets they had been chastened only in moderation.

Symmachus says: "They became unstable, blind in the exits; they were befouled with blood, so that no one could touch their clothing." Scripture calls the angels "watchers," as in Daniel. These were perhaps the ones through whom the law was given by Moses, according to "For if the law spoken through angels." So these, who had been attending on the city and on the divine temple, were shaken and departed. For Josephus relates in his account of the capture that "at night the priests went into the temple, as was their custom for the services, and said that they first perceived a movement, and after that a voice of many crying together, 'Let us depart from here.'" It was then that, in Symmachus's words, they became unstable and wanderers, and "blind," he says, "in the exits." For "there was no vision giving direction, no prophet, nor leader"; they failed when "he came for whom it was reserved, who was the expectation of the nations."

He commands the apostles to flee from the midst of the Jews, who were defiled with the blood of Christ, and he also entrusted the calling out to them to the angels. Or perhaps he bids the apostles call them, unclean as they are, to repentance, which they did, saying, "It was necessary that the word be spoken to you first." But when they refused, he orders the apostles to flee; that is why they say, as to those who are unwilling, "Behold, we turn to the Gentiles."

"They were kindled" signifies the fire of the capture; "they were shaken," the removal into slavery; and "they shall no longer sojourn," that they will have a perpetual sojourning and will never need a second one.

It signifies the punishment that comes from Christ, for David says, "The face of the Lord is against those who do evil." They are not looked upon by him while they remain what they are; for "when the full number of the Gentiles has come in, all Israel will be saved," and thereafter as faithful [?]. If the text should read "their portion," clearly he is speaking of those who go out from the midst. As for the enemies, they did not respect the face of the priests, for they led them all away.

The words seem to come from the captives, repenting that they had relied on the Egyptians and Assyrians for help. They could also fittingly be spoken by those of the circumcision who believed: "We failed, hoping in vain in the law"; for the law saves no one, as Paul said. So neither will those who cling to the law be able to help after grace has come.

For those whom the Saviour appointed "fishers of men" hunted Jews who were infants in mind, so that they would not walk the broad and spacious way of their fathers. It was to these that the Saviour alluded when he said, "Let the children come to me."

For Josephus relates that not even the mountains saved those who fled. There, then, dragging us away, they "were kindled," that is, they were inflamed against us to punish us. It could also be understood of the apostles, whose "youth was renewed like the eagle's."

Some have said that in these special verses he laments Josiah more plainly. For they hoped that through his piety Jerusalem would be raised to glory in the midst of the nations, since Jerusalem lies in the midst of the nations. And he, they say, is a type of Christ, having died for the iniquities of the people. Yet he was not taken in the people's corruptions, but because he went out to meet Pharaoh Neco though the prophet forbade it, even though Neco did not want to fight him. So, according to the divine apostle, "a veil lies on the face of the Jews when Moses is read; but when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed; now the Lord is the Spirit." And through the prophet he calls the Lord "spirit." Those on whom the veil lies would not say, "The breath of our face is Christ the Lord"; rather, those would say it who "with unveiled face behold as in a mirror the glory of the Lord," and before the eyes of whose mind the Lord always stands. Thus it is clear that the Spirit that worked in the prophets was Christ, who, having become man, also says, "I who speak am here," being himself spirit and Lord and Christ. He was seized by those who had first corrupted the seeds of piety in themselves. "But we, the prophets, regarding no other as the breath of our face, and having no longer any place among them after our capture, shall live under the shadow of Christ, no longer among the Jews but among all the nations," when "the kingdom of God, taken from them" because of their outrage against Christ, "was given to the nations." For behold, the prophets live among [?], speaking of him and proclaiming him, but no longer among those who even now surround him with their corruptions and blaspheme him daily. Aquila said, "the breath of our nostrils," and Symmachus, "the breathing of our nostrils." For those who love God breathe Christ continually, having him before their eyes. It must be understood that just as Christ, being spirit, spoke in the prophets, so did the Father, for Paul says in Hebrews: "In many parts and in many ways God spoke of old in the prophets; in these last days he has spoken to us in a Son." So too did the Holy Spirit, for the Saviour says, "Well did the Holy Spirit say in Isaiah: You will indeed hear and never understand." And in Corinthians Paul, after listing the gifts, among which is prophecy, says, "All these are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as it wills"—that is, with sovereign authority, not as a servant. You might call Christ "the breath of our face" as the one who gave us the spirit of prophecy. For prophecy is the face of the prophets, the spirit is the gift, and the shadow is the law, "for the law has a shadow of the good things to come." So the prophets lived among us and in the shadow of the law. The prophetic gift, then, toward which the outcome of all prophecy looks, is Christ, that is, it comes from Christ, "for Christ is the end of the law and the prophets." It might also be spoken in the person of the apostles and the faithful: "For in him we live and move and have our being"; of him we said, "In his shadow we shall live," that is, by imitating him. For the divine apostle says, "Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ."

The words are addressed to the people of Edom and of Esau, the brother of Jacob, foretelling an excess of evils for them (for this is what "you will be drunk and pour out" means). David also speaks of them: "Remember, O Lord, the sons of Edom on the day of Jerusalem, who said, 'Empty it, empty it, down to its foundation.'" For though they were brothers and neighbours, they kept up the hatred of their ancestors. Having spoken about Christ, he fittingly mentioned Edom too. For Christ was going to lay waste the one called "Earthy," making it heavenly. Virtue and knowledge are a threat to those who delight in errors and passions; for them, drunkenness is the putting to death of the flesh, and pouring out is the putting to death of the mind of the flesh.

You have paid a sufficient penalty, and in it Edom will take your place. "He will no longer carry you into exile" is said either with reference to the recall (for you will not remain in captivity once you have filled up the full measure; God lessens the penalty and does not add to it), or else it refers to a second capture that would not happen; but then how did the later capture by the Romans take place? Perhaps, then, the words concern the last capture, which happened because of Christ, after which there has been no other. And all Israel, having abandoned its iniquity, will be saved after the full number of the [Gentiles] has come in. After that comes the consummation and the punishment of the earthly, with the judgment to follow. The words could also be addressed to the church, which is the daughter of the ancient synagogue ("for the gifts of God are irrevocable," and her iniquity came to an end through divine baptism). He no longer hands her over to her enemies, he who said, "Here I will dwell, for I have chosen her," and "Behold, I am with you all the days until the end of the age." At that time he also publicly denounced the impiety of those whose minds are set on earthly things.
